rule: good. the bare plural subject becomes a rule giving every cliff-spire its own shielding of the Northcove, cliff_spire exposes just its head genus, and the Northcove gets a stable symbol plus exactly one name fact.
texts: good. every part of the condition binds through plain variables, so the rule genuinely fires, and the spires, the cove, the north winds, the cove's lanterns, the manner "stably" and the winter span are all carried; the only quibble is that "from north winds" lands in the spatial Source slot rather than a plain "from" oblique, which costs nothing here.

bad: the rule can never fire — the spires and the blocking are written as constructed terms (sk_spires $c) and (sk_block $c) inside the condition, and those match nothing in the knowledge base, so no real blocking ever sets it off. The trouble is the indefinite "a cove" buried in a from-phrase that the second clause then points back at; put the cove up front as the condition clause's subject instead: "When a cove is blocked from the north wind by cliff-spires, the lanterns in that cove stay lit through winter."

bad: "the cove of Aelmere" is recorded with PartOf, which is reserved for a component of an object or a member of a group and is expressly barred for one place inside another, and the identificational "is THE shielded cove" — the claim that this is Aelmere's only shielded cove — is dropped without trace. State the location plainly: "The Northcove is a shielded cove in Aelmere." If the uniqueness matters it needs its own sentence, because a definite predicate nominal has no carrier at all.

good. "never" gives a strength-0 rule with the surface word recorded, the place name attaches to the lanterns by the loose possession link prescribed for a name premodifying a common noun, "go out" is kept whole as a phrasal verb, and cold winds now vary per binding instead of collapsing into one wind.
